text: Now we're 25, 30 years into the Internet, 25 years since, like, almost everybody knew what it was, and proliferation of bandwidth. And now we're all connected to this network, everyone, every human being. We get a chance to ask the question about whether the Internet that we have today is the very best version of what it could be. I would argue that crypto is asking a lot of those questions at this point. I mean, there's not more than five or six companies that are controlling most of our time on the Internet and making most of the money. I don't think that's a good thing, and I don't think that's natural. I don't think it's, like, evolutionary. It's more corporate network effects. I think crypto is the first shot to kind of start to build things that are owned by the community and can stand the test of time and are not taking our rights and our money and our freedom. That part makes me excited to work in the industry, because I just think we're building better things. You have to accept the fact that there's also a lot of terrible things that are built in crypto, but inside of that chaos, there's, like, real interesting, cool things that are going to be awesome for humanity. As long as you're willing to see through that noise. I really think that we're crafting a set of Protestant experiences that, like, most of humanity will be enjoying within probably a decade.
